title: Feeling Good: The New Mood Therapy
author: David D. Burns, M.D.
edition_analyzed: Revised and updated edition (most widely available paperback)
target_audience: Individuals struggling with depression, anxiety, or negative moods
Readers seeking practical strategies for emotional self-help
Anyone interested in cognitive behavioral approaches to mood management
core_themes: Understanding the causes of depression and negative moods
The relationship between thoughts, feelings, and behaviors
Developing self-acceptance and healthier patterns of thinking
primary_purpose: To empower readers to recognize, confront, and reverse depressive thinking patterns through Cognitive Behavioral Therapy techniques, thereby improving overall mental health without the immediate need for medication.

structure_format.narrative_style: Conversational, explanatory, and supportive; accessible to lay readers
structure_format.organization: Divided into thematic chapters with step-by-step exercises, illustrative case studies, and self-assessment tools
features: Illustrative patient stories and case examples
Summaries of key concepts at the end of chapters

key_concepts_lessons: Depressive feelings often stem from distorted, automatic negative thoughts.
Common distortions include all-or-nothing thinking, overgeneralization, and emotional reasoning.
Thoughts, emotions, and behaviors are interrelated; changing thoughts can shift emotions.
Self-monitoring and specific CBT techniques can reduce and prevent relapses into depression.
You can regain control over your mood by practicing cognitive restructuring, activity scheduling, and realistic self-talk.
Medication is not always necessary—CBT can be highly effective as a first-line intervention for many.
notable_features: Pioneering mainstream introduction to Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for the public
Step-by-step, actionable techniques for mood improvement
Emphasis on reader practice and self-application
Widely recommended by therapists and health practitioners
cultural_historical_context: Published in 1980, 'Feeling Good' marked a major shift towards acceptance of cognitive therapy among both professionals and the general public, providing a practical, non-stigmatizing alternative to medication during a period when mental health stigma was high.
reception_impact: Over 5 million copies sold; enduring bestseller in self-help and mental health
Recommended reading by many therapists, psychiatrists, and mental health organizations
Significantly contributed to the popularization and acceptance of CBT worldwide
Praised for clarity, practical guidance, and empathy toward depression sufferers
Some critics suggest further reading or professional guidance is needed for severe cases
comparable_titles: The Feeling Good Handbook by David D. Burns
Mind Over Mood by Dennis Greenberger and Christine A. Padesky
Learned Optimism by Martin E.P. Seligman
